blocks.h: EVERYONE AT THE PARTY WATCHED ME LEAVE
Roya Publication No. 100
by Chew Z
HERE BE DELOS

On the oldest maps, the edge of the known world was marked with a warning. Where the mapmakers had been, they drew coastlines and rivers and towns. Where they had not been, they wrote a few words in Latin: hic sunt leones [HEEK soont lay-OH-nays], here are lions. On one small copper globe, made around the year 1510, somebody wrote something stranger along the far coast of Asia: hic sunt dracones [HEEK soont drah-KOH-nays], here are dragons. It is almost the only place in the world those words have ever been found. The famous English saying, here be dragons, grew out of them later. Here be is simply an old way of saying here are.
These books keep the mapmaker’s warning and change the creature.

Delos [DEE-los] is a Greek word. It means clear, visible, plain to see. It is also the second half of a word you know. In 1956 a British psychiatrist named Humphry Osmond needed a name for a family of substances that change the mind, and he built one out of two Greek words: psyche [SY-kee], the mind or soul, and delos, made visible. Psychedelic. Mind-manifesting. Not a poison and not an escape, he meant, but something that shows the mind to itself.
And Delos is an island.

The old Greek story says that the goddess Leto was going to have a child by Zeus, the king of the gods, and that Zeus’s wife, Hera, in her fury, forbade every land on earth to give Leto a place to give birth. Every land was afraid, and every land said no. But there was one place that did not count as land. It was a small island that had once been Leto’s own sister, who had leapt from the sky into the sea like a falling star, and it had been drifting ever since, loose on the water, fixed to nothing, and so hard to see that nobody could find it. Because it was not fixed to the earth, Hera’s command could not reach it. It took Leto in.
There, on the drifting island, in hiding, she gave birth to Apollo, the god of light.

And the island stopped drifting. The poets say that four great pillars rose up out of the sea floor and held it still. A Greek poet named Callimachus [kuh-LIM-uh-kus], writing more than two thousand years ago, tells us why it got its name: because it no longer drifted unseen on the water, but had put down roots in the middle of the sea. The sailors called it Delos. The one that can be seen.
Hidden first. Then fixed, and seen.

That is what every book in this series does. Each one follows a single person, and a single substance from somewhere in the world, a leaf, a seed, a root, a mushroom, a molecule, that moves through that person’s life without a name, drifting, hidden, doing its work in the dark. And then, when the story has earned it, it is named. It stops drifting. And the book tells you everything about it: where it grows, who found it, what its names mean, what it does to the brain, what it has been used for, and what it costs.
Inside the book is a map of the world. It begins as scribble. This book fixes the first place on it.
Here be Delos. Here is the place made visible.
SYNOPSIS
It is a Saturday night in April 2007, and Tomás is twenty years old, sitting on the carpet of a fraternity-house bedroom in Los Angeles with his back against the bed, waiting to leave.

For two years he has felt nothing. A doctor gave it a name and a prescription; the pills made the flatness quieter, but it is still there, like living behind a window. So when his friend Danny holds up a small printed bag from a smoke shop on the boulevard and asks who will try what is inside it, on camera, at the party, Tomás says yes. People say it takes the mind to the strangest place it can go. If even that cannot reach him, he will know.
He spends the week reading about it in the dark and makes Danny promise to stay sober and hold the camera. He is careful not to learn its name. He wants to be surprised.
The camera’s counter begins at zero. The last thing Tomás sees before the room folds shut is the small red light on the front of it.
What he finds on the other side is a dirt floor, a tin roof in the rain, and a barefoot boy of seven, counting leaves in the dark, who has been waiting for him for a very long time.
The boy has lost something. He needs help to find it.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

This book begins with Terence McKenna. I never met him. I heard him, the way most people did, as a voice on a recording, and what stayed with me was not any one of his ideas but the way he said them. He could take an experience that most of his listeners had never had, and that the people who had had it swore could not be put into words, and he would put it into words — plain ones, funny ones, exact ones — until a stranger could stand inside it. He treated language as the one instrument we have for carrying something back from a place nobody else can visit. I have tried to hold these pages to that. Where the experience cannot be described, I have tried to describe it anyway, honestly, and to say where the words run out. This book is dedicated to him, and to the power of words to describe the indescribable.

The title of this series comes from a map and an island, and the page before this one tells the story. What the island means to me is simple. We all carry places we have stopped looking at: rooms we have closed, people we have not mourned. They drift out there, unseen. Now and then something makes one of them visible, and fixes it, and we have to decide whether to look.

I chose this leaf first because it is, for its size, the strangest door I know of, and because it belongs to a living people who have kept it, carefully and by hand, for longer than anyone can say. The Mazatec of Oaxaca did not invent it for parties, and this book is not a guide to taking it. The people and the story are invented. The plant, its history, its science and its dangers are as true as I could make them, checked against the people who studied it most closely, who are named at the back.
There is a word in this book, susto, that names a kind of grief. Tomás learns it from a child. I learned it late, too.
Chew Z
I. THE DARE
Minute 0:00. It is Sunday morning, and Danny’s camera is on my knees.

He left it outside my door before he went to breakfast, with a note on a paper towel that says you should see this. I have made coffee I have not drunk. I have folded out the little screen on the side of the camera and pressed play, and a counter has appeared in the corner, white numbers on black: zero minutes, zero seconds.

On the screen is a room, and in the room is me. The tape runs for thirty-four minutes. I am going to watch all of it, and while I watch, I am going to tell you where I really was, because the tape cannot. I will use the counter to tell you where we are. Every time the story moves, I will tell you what it says.
Here is where the tape begins.

It was a Saturday night in April 2007, and I was twenty years old, and I was sitting on the carpet in Danny Reyes’s bedroom on the second floor of a fraternity house, with my back against his bed, waiting to leave.
That is the plainest way I know to begin, so I will begin there, and I will go slowly, because the rest of this is not plain at all, and you will need something to stand on.

Danny had just switched on the camera. It was a small silver video camera, the size of a paperback, and he had set it on his desk on top of two chemistry textbooks so that it would be level with my face. On the front of it there was a red light. When he pressed the button, the numbers began to move. One second. Two.
I did not know it then, but that counter was going to be the only thing I could trust for the next half hour.

Minute 0:20. Below us the party was loud. You could feel it more than hear it: the bass coming up through the floor into the carpet and into the bones of my hands. Someone downstairs was shouting a name over and over, happily. A girl was laughing on the landing. The house smelled of spilled beer, cheap cologne and the pizza boxes stacked by the front door since Thursday.

Danny’s room was the room of a boy who had moved out of his parents’ house eighteen months before and had not yet understood that nobody else was going to clean it. A futon with a broken leg, propped on a dictionary. A poster of a band he had stopped liking. A small refrigerator humming in the corner. On the desk, beside the camera, a glass pipe, a yellow plastic lighter, and a small printed bag, folded over at the top, about the size of a packet of sugar.
I had not looked at the bag. I want you to know that. I had made a point of not looking at it.
Minute 0:45. Here is how I came to be on the floor.
On Monday night, five days before, Danny had carried his laptop into the kitchen of the house, where ten or twelve of us were eating cereal for dinner, and said, “You have to see this.”

On the screen was a video, a few minutes long, the kind that people were passing around that spring. A young man in a dormitory room, sitting in a desk chair. Someone off camera handed him a glass pipe. He breathed in from it, handed it back, and looked at the wall.

For a few seconds nothing happened. Then his face changed. I don’t know how else to say it. It was as if the person who lived behind his face had stepped out of the room and left the lights on. He stared at the wall. He began to laugh, not at anything, just laughing, and then he slid slowly sideways out of the chair, onto the floor, and lay there talking to the carpet in a soft, reasonable voice, as if he were explaining something important to it.
The kitchen howled. Somebody spat cereal. Danny played it twice more.

Then he said that he had the stuff. That was the word he used: the stuff. He had bought it that afternoon, he said, at a smoke shop on the boulevard, over the counter, perfectly legal, twenty-five dollars. He wanted to film one of us doing it at the party on Saturday. He had a new camera and he wanted a reason to use it.
“Who’s in?” he said.
Nobody said anything. Then everyone looked at me, because I was the one who never did anything, and they were waiting for me to say no so they could laugh at that instead.
I said yes.
Minute 1:10. I should tell you why, and I should tell you the true reason, not the one I gave in the kitchen.
In the kitchen I said, “Somebody has to be the scientist.” That got a laugh. It was the kind of thing I was known for saying.
The true reason is that for two years I had not felt anything.

I don’t mean I was sad. Sad is a feeling. I mean that the world had gone flat, the way a soda goes flat, still the same color, still the same shape, but with nothing moving inside it. I went to class. I got good grades. I laughed at the right times. I could tell you exactly what a joke was supposed to feel like, the way you can describe the taste of a food you ate once as a child. But I could not taste it. It was like living behind a window. Everything was there. I could see all of it. I could not touch any of it.

In the autumn of my first year I had gone to the student health center and sat in a small room with a kind doctor who asked me questions from a sheet of paper, and at the end of the sheet she had a word for it. The word was depression. She gave me a prescription. The pills made the window quieter. They did not open it.

So when Danny said that this was the strangest thing a human mind could do, and that people came back from it unable to say where they had been, I thought: good. Show me somewhere strange enough, and I will know whether there is anyone left in here to be surprised.
That is what I mean when I say I came to the party for the strangeness. I was not looking for fun. I was looking for proof.
Minute 1:40. For the rest of that week, at night, after my roommate was asleep, I read about it.

I read on forums where strangers wrote long reports of what had happened to them, under names like Nightwalker and DeepBlue, with dates at the top and times written down to the minute. I read them the way some people read ghost stories: in the dark, with the covers up, a little ashamed of how much I wanted to believe them.

I learned that these people had their own way of saying how strong something had been. They used plus signs. One plus meant I could tell it was working, but I couldn’t tell you how. Two plus meant I knew exactly what it was doing, and I could still choose what to do about it. Three plus meant I could not ignore it any more; it was the only thing happening. And four plus, which almost nobody claimed, meant something that could not be described at all, a place you might go once in your life and never find again. The scale, somebody wrote, had been made up by a chemist in California who had spent his life trying to write down things that could not be written down. I liked him for that.
I started a notebook. On the first page I wrote Plus four or I want a refund, and I underlined it, because I was twenty and I thought I was funny.
Minute 2:15. There was one rule that every report repeated, whatever else it said. It was said so many times, by so many strangers who agreed on nothing else, that it began to feel like a prayer.

Have someone with you who has taken nothing. Sit down on the floor, somewhere you cannot fall. Take away anything sharp, anything glass, anything you could walk into. Because for a few minutes, the reports said, you will not know that your body exists, and your body will not know that you are gone, and it may decide to get up and go for a walk without you.

I read that sentence three times. Then I went to Danny’s room at one in the morning and woke him up and made him promise: no beer on Saturday until it was over. He would stay sober. He would hold the camera. He would not let me stand up.
“You’re a weird guy, Tomás,” he said, with his eyes closed.
“Promise,” I said.
He promised. And I will say this for Danny Reyes, who was loud and careless about nearly everything: he kept it.
Minute 2:50. There was one thing I did not read.

I did not read the name on the bag. I did not look up what the stuff was called, or what it came from, or where it grew. Every time a report used its real name, I let my eyes slide past the word, the way you look away from the last page of a mystery when you pick it up in a shop.
I told myself it was because I wanted to be surprised. That if I knew too much about it, my own mind would do the work, and I would never know what was the stuff and what was me.
That was true. It was not the whole truth. But I did not know the whole truth yet, and neither, at this point, do you. We are going to find it out together, and I am not going to jump ahead.

Minute 3:20. While Danny fussed with the lamp, trying to get the light right, I thought about my family. I did not mean to. It happened the way it happens when you are nervous and trying to seem calm.

I thought about my mother, at home in our apartment in the east of the city, who would be asleep by now in front of the television, with her shoes still on. My mother came from a village in the mountains of Oaxaca [wah-HAH-kah], a state in the south of Mexico, a place so high that the clouds come into the houses in the morning and have to be let out again. Her people are Mazatec [MAH-zah-tek], an old people of those mountains, with their own language, older than Spanish.

I was born in that village. I lived there until I was seven, with my mother and my grandmother, in a house with a dirt floor and a blue door. Then my mother brought me north, to Los Angeles, and I never went back. When people asked me why, I said I didn’t remember much about it, and I changed the subject.

I thought about my grandmother, my abuela [ah-BWEH-lah], who had died three years before, when I was seventeen. I had not gone to the funeral. My mother went, alone, and came back a week later and did not talk about it, and I did not ask.

And I thought, for about one second, about my father, which is about as long as I ever thought about him. My father went north to find work when I was six. He was going to get a job, save money, and send for us. For a while he called. Then he stopped calling. My mother has told me the same thing, in the same words, for thirteen years: He left us. He had another life somewhere. He did not want us.
I believed her. I hated him for it, in the easy, finished way you hate someone you cannot remember. I thought it was the one thing about my life that I had completely understood.
I put all of that away, the way you put things in a drawer before guests arrive, and I looked at the camera.

Minute 3:45. By now there were people in the doorway. Two of the brothers, one of them a tall boy from Sacramento whose name I have never been able to remember, and a girl in a green sweater who had followed them up the stairs to see what the noise was about. They leaned on the door frame with their drinks, grinning, the way people grin at the start of a video they have already seen the end of.

Danny had moved the lamp, the desk chair and a beer bottle out of reach. He had pushed the futon against the wall. He had cleared a space on the carpet about the size of a bathtub, and I sat in the middle of it with my back against the side of the bed and my legs crossed.
I looked into the camera, into the red light, and I said, “Plus four or I want a refund.”
They laughed. Danny laughed. The girl in the green sweater said, “What does that mean?” and nobody answered her.

Danny unfolded the top of the little bag. He did not show it to me and I did not ask to see it. He did what he needed to do at the desk with his back to me, and then he knelt down on the carpet and held out the glass pipe and the yellow lighter, and said, very quietly, so the others could not hear, “I’ve got you, man. I’m right here.”
Minute 4:10. The last thing I looked at before I breathed in was the red light on the camera.

I want to tell you exactly what happened next, second by second, as well as I can. I am going to fail. I know that now. But I am going to fail slowly and carefully, so that you can see the shape of what I am failing to describe.
I breathed in. It tasted of burnt leaves, bitter and hot, like the smoke from a garden bonfire in autumn. I handed the pipe back to
Danny. I remember that I was careful not to drop it.

For a moment, nothing. I sat there with the taste in my mouth and the music coming up through the floor and four people looking at me, and I thought: well, that’s that, then. Nothing. Of course nothing.
Minute 4:18. Then the music went flat.

Not quieter. Flat. As if the sound had been printed onto a sheet of paper and the sheet had been laid down on the floor. I could still hear every note. But the notes no longer came from anywhere. They were just there, lying on the carpet around me, the way light lies on a floor.
Minute 4:25. The carpet under my hands began to slide to the left.

I knew it was not moving. I could see that it was not moving. But I could feel it moving, slowly and steadily, the way a train beside yours in a station seems to start moving when it is really you. I pressed my hands down harder to hold it still, and it went on sliding, politely, underneath them.
Minute 4:31. Then the edge of the room began to fold.
This is the first thing I will ask you to picture, so I will give you three ways in, and none of them is quite right.

It was like a page of a book being turned toward me, very slowly, by a hand I could not see: the far wall of Danny’s bedroom lifting up off the floor at its bottom edge and curling over toward me, with the poster and the window and the door still on it.
It was like lying on your back in a swimming pool and watching the side of the pool bend over you, the way things bend when you look up at them through water.
It was like the moment in a dream when you realize the house you are standing in is also a different house, and both of them are true.
It was none of those things. It was the room, folding, with me inside it.
I tried to say it’s starting. I heard the words come out of my mouth in the wrong order, and each word landed on the carpet, separately, like coins.
Minute 4:40. The only thing in the room that did not move was the red light on the camera.

I held on to it with my eyes. Everything else was turning over — the wall, the door, the faces in the doorway, the ceiling — like a page, like a wave, like a lid. And in the middle of all of it, one small red light, perfectly still, perfectly round, perfectly patient, the way a star is still when everything below it is weather.
I remember thinking, very clearly: as long as I can see the red light, I am still here.
Then the page turned over the red light too, and I was not.
II. THE WALL

Minute 4:41. On the screen on my knees, the young man on the carpet has gone quiet. His eyes are open. He is looking at nothing in particular, the way you look at a window when you are thinking about something else. His hands are flat on the carpet on either side of him. He looks calm. He looks, if anything, a little bored.
That is what the tape shows. Here is where I was.
Minute 4:44. I was flat.

I mean that exactly. I had no front and no back. I had width and I had height and that was all. I was a surface, and I was facing out into the room, and I understood, slowly and without any alarm at all, that I was the wall.

Not in the wall. Not looking at the wall. I was the wall of Danny’s bedroom, the one with the window in it, and I could feel the poster taped to me like a sticking plaster, and the window set into me like a coin set into dough, and the cold of the April night pressing on my back from outside.

I want to say that this was frightening, and later it was. But in that first moment it felt as normal as having hands. Of course I was the wall. I had always been the wall. It was the rest of my life that suddenly seemed strange, all that walking around.
Minute 4:49. Here are three ways to picture it. None of them is right.
It was like the moment in a cartoon when a character is run over by a steamroller and peels himself up off the road, flat as paper, and still has his own face.
It was like being a photograph of yourself, printed on the side of a building, and knowing, from the inside of the paper, which way the wind was blowing.
It was like being very, very thin ice on a pond, with the whole of the weather on one side and the whole of the water on the other, and nothing of you in between but a single held breath.
It was none of those things. I was the wall, and the wall was comfortable, and that is the part I still cannot explain.
Minute 4:53. Then I noticed the colors.

Danny’s room was painted a tired beige. In the light of his desk lamp it had always looked like the inside of an old envelope. Now the beige had come apart into its ingredients, the way white light comes apart in a prism, except that what came out of it were not the colors of a rainbow. They were the colors of things.

There was a yellow that was exactly the yellow of the plastic lighter. There was a green that was the green of a school hallway. There was a pink like the inside of a cheek. And they were not lying flat on the wall, which was me; they were moving across me in slow bands, the way the stripes move on a barber’s pole, always climbing and never arriving.

The strangest thing was that I could feel the colors as temperatures. The yellow was warm, like a hand on the back of the neck. The green was cool, like a coin. The pink was the temperature of a body. I was not seeing color any more. I was being touched by it.
Minute 4:58. Then the room began to curve.

In an ordinary room, the lines are straight. The edge where the wall meets the ceiling is a straight line. The edge of the desk is a straight line. The door frame is two straight lines and a third across the top. You have never once thought about this, because straight lines are what rooms are made of.

Now every straight line in the room had begun, very slowly, to bend in the same direction, like the lines on a page when you hold the page up and curl it toward you. The ceiling bent down to meet me. The floor bent up. The two side walls leaned in from the left and the right. And all of the lines were bending around the same point, as if the whole room were being rolled up, gently, into a tube, and I was the paper at the center of the roll.
I could see the edges of the room joining up behind me, where no eyes could see, and I knew what was there as clearly as you know where your own feet are in the dark.
Minute 5:02. The room was not only curving. It was turning.

It turned the way a wheel turns: steadily, all in one direction, without any sound. The poster came round, and the door, and the desk with the red light on it, and the doorway with the three faces in it, and then the poster again. It was like sitting in the middle of a revolving door that never lets you out. It was like being the axle of a bicycle wheel and watching the spokes go past. It was like the drum of a washing machine, seen from the inside, very slowly, with the whole of Danny’s room tumbling in it like laundry.

And the turning had a pull. That is the word every report I read that week had used, and I had not understood it until then. Something was pulling me to the left. Not a hand. Not wind. A steady, patient, enormous pull, like a current in the sea, or like the way a magnet pulls a pin across a table: not violently, but with complete certainty that the pin is going to end up where the magnet is.
Minute 5:05. On the tape, at this point, I start to laugh.

I have just watched it three times. The young man on the carpet begins to laugh, quietly at first, a little snort through the nose, and then more, and then so much that he folds forward over his own knees and his shoulders shake. The girl in the green sweater laughs too, because laughing is catching, and Danny’s voice, just off the screen, says, “Dude. Dude. What’s funny?”
I know what was funny. I will try to tell you, and it will not be funny when I tell it.

What was funny was that the pull was so serious. It was so large and so patient and so completely sure of itself, and there I was, a wall, with a poster stuck on me, being pulled. The size of the thing and the smallness of me were so far apart that the only possible answer was to laugh, the way you laugh when a very small dog barks at a very large truck.

And under the laughter, there was something else, which I did not have a word for yet. It was the feeling you get at the top of the stairs in your own house in the dark, when you reach for the last step and it is not there. A drop in the stomach. Not fear, exactly. The shape of fear, before the fear arrives.
Minute 5:09. Then the sound came apart.

I told you the music had gone flat, like a sheet of paper laid on the floor. Now the paper was being rolled up with the rest of the room, and the sound was curving too. I could hear the bass from downstairs, but it was coming from behind me and in front of me at the same moment, the way the sea sounds when you hold a shell to your ear. I could hear the girl in the green sweater laughing, but her laugh was the color pink, and it was moving across me in a band with the other colors.

And underneath all of it, a hum. One steady note, very low, like the note a refrigerator makes in an empty kitchen at night, the note you only notice when it stops. It was everywhere. It was the sound the turning made. I understood that it had always been there, under every other sound I had ever heard, and that I had never once been quiet enough to hear it.
Minute 5:13. Here is the part the tape shows most clearly, and I understand it least.

On the screen, the young man stops laughing. All at once, as if a switch had been turned. He sits up straight. He puts both hands out in front of him, palms down, and pushes, slowly, at the air, as if he were pushing against a pane of glass that no one else can see. His face is very serious. He is looking at something to the left of the camera.
Where I was, the turning had become a set of pages.

I don’t know how else to say this. The room was no longer a wheel. It was a book, a thick one, lying open, and I was one of the pages, and something was turning the pages one at a time, from right to left, and every page was a room. Danny’s room, with me on the wall. Then the same room, empty. Then the same room with the lamp in a different place. Then a room I had never seen, with green tiles. Then a bus shelter in the rain. Then a hospital corridor. Then a white room with nothing in it but a window.

Each page turned over me and pressed me flat and moved on, and I was pressed flat into each room in turn, and for as long as the page lay on me I was that room: its walls, its air, its light. And then the next page came over.
I was pushing at them. That is what the tape shows. I was trying to hold the pages still.
Minute 5:18. I want to tell you about time here, because this is where it broke.

You have been reading these little numbers, the ones the counter shows. Four minutes and forty-four seconds. Five minutes and eighteen seconds. Between those two numbers, thirty-four seconds passed in Danny’s bedroom. I know that because the tape says so, and a tape cannot lie about that.
Inside, I do not know how long it was. It was not long, and it was not short. It was like asking how long a smell lasts, or how heavy a color is. The question did not fit.

The pages were turning, one room after another, and some of them turned in the time it takes to blink, and some of them lay on me for what felt like a whole afternoon. In one of them it was raining the whole time. In one of them it was night and then morning, and I watched the window go from black to grey to white, and that was one page.

If you have ever woken in the night and not known, for a second, what day it is, or where the door is, or how old you are, you have been in the doorway of this. I was all the way through the door, and it had closed behind me, and I had no idea any more which side of it was the real one.
Minute 5:24. And then I was afraid.

Not the shape of fear this time. The real thing. It came up from the bottom of me like water filling a room, and it had one clear thought in it, the only clear thought I had had since I breathed in: I have been here before.

Not in Danny’s room. Not in any of the pages. In this feeling. In being small and flat and pressed against a wall in the dark, while something enormous happened in the middle of the room, and I could not move, and I could not look away, and I could not make a sound.

I did not know where that feeling came from. I knew only that it was old, much older than the party, older than Los Angeles, and that it had been waiting for me at the back of this place the way a dog waits at a door.
On the tape, the young man on the carpet has gone very still. His hands have dropped to his lap. Danny’s voice, much quieter now, says, “Tomás? You good?”
I did not hear him. I was being pulled, harder now, to the left, through the last of the pages.
Minute 5:29. The last page was dark.

It was not black, the way a room is black with the lights off. It was dark the way the country is dark, with no street lamps for miles: a deep, blue, soft dark that you can see into once your eyes stop fighting it.
The pull stopped. The turning stopped. Even the hum sank away, somewhere far beneath everything, and in the space where it had been, I heard something I had not heard in thirteen years.
Rain on a tin roof.
And under it, very close, a small sound, patient and regular, like someone counting under their breath.
III. THE BOY IN THE KITCHEN
Minute 5:30. I was lying on my side on a floor.

It was not carpet. I knew that before I knew anything else, because my cheek was on it, and it was cool and a little damp and gave very slightly under my weight, the way a garden path gives after rain. WHAT IT DID
Salvia divinorum, the leaf of the Shepherdess. Grown. A plant of the mint family, known only from the mountains of the Sierra Mazateca in Oaxaca, Mexico. Door: leaving the body.

How it was taken in this book. Once, as a concentrated extract sold in a smoke shop, breathed in from a glass pipe. Not the traditional way, which is to chew the fresh leaves slowly, at night, in darkness and silence, with someone watching.
How long. It began within seconds. The strongest part lasted a few minutes. By about half an hour it was over. Inside, it felt far longer.
What it did to time. Time came loose. A few real minutes held what felt like a whole night, and thirteen years.
What it did to the body. He lost it. He became a flat surface, part of a wall. His body, left behind, laughed, cried, stood up and walked toward a window, and was stopped by a friend.
What it did to the self. He met a boy, and learned that the boy was himself: the part of him left behind at seven, on the night his father’s death was spoken aloud.

What it did to the world. Colors separated and were felt as warmth and cold. Straight lines bent. The room rolled up and turned like a wheel, then like the pages of a book. A low hum under everything. Then a kitchen in the mountains, and a room he had not let himself remember.
What it meant. He felt that something true was being shown to him. The leaf did not know anything or cure anything. It opened a door he had nailed shut.
What it did not do. It did not heal him. The next morning he was still the person with the doctor’s word and the pills. He knew where the lost piece was. That is not the same as having it back.

THE MAPMAKER
For Daniel Siebert (1963–2024)
In 1993, in Southern California, a young man sat down to find out whether a white powder could open a door.

The powder was salvinorin A [sal-vih-NOR-in AY], a substance taken out of the leaves of Salvia divinorum. Chemists in Mexico had first separated it from the leaf in 1982, and another team had found it again two years later. They knew it was there. What nobody knew was whether it was the thing in the leaf that did the work. For thirty years, ever since the first outsiders had come down the mountain with the leaf in 1962, scientists had tried to find the part of it that took the mind somewhere else, and failed. The Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann, who had found so many other doors, had tried and failed. The juice he had carried home from Mexico had lost its power. The door stayed closed.

Daniel Siebert was an ethnobotanist, someone who studies how people use plants, and a careful, curious man who had spent years growing the leaf and learning everything the Mazatec healers and the handful of scientists who had visited them had written down. He had a small amount of the pure substance, and a question, and the courage, or the curiosity, to answer it the only way it could be answered then.
He tried a tiny amount of it on himself, with friends watching over him. Within seconds, the room was gone.

He published what he had found in June 1994, in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology, under a plain title: Salvia divinorum and salvinorin A: new pharmacologic findings (volume 43, pages 53–56). It was the first proof that this one substance, and not something else, was the key in the leaf. And it showed something no one had expected: that it was extraordinarily strong. Amounts too small to see were enough. By weight, it was the most powerful mind-changing substance known to grow anywhere in nature.

That was the beginning of everything else. Once the key was known, scientists could go looking for the lock. In 2002, a team led by the American pharmacologist Bryan Roth found it: a lock in the brain that no plant like this had ever been known to touch, the kappa-opioid receptor. The leaf had shown the scientists a door in the mind they had not known was there.

Siebert spent the rest of his life on the leaf. He started a centre for information about it, and helped publish a guide for people who were going to take it anyway, which put safety first: have a sober sitter with you, put away anything dangerous, lie down, never drive. He talked to newspapers and television when the videos began to spread, and asked people to understand what the plant was before they banned it or bought it. In 2002 he spoke against a bill in the United States Congress that would have made the leaf illegal everywhere in the country. He believed it should be respected, not feared, and not sold as a joke. He died in 2024.

This book is dedicated to him, because he was the first person to know for certain what was in the leaf that opened the door, and because he spent the rest of his life asking people to be careful with it.
